title.en: Say what a deformation animation claims

summary: Distinguish an animation that demonstrates a continuous deformation from one that merely morphs between two shapes.
objective: Keep morphing animations from implying topological equivalences they do not establish.
applies_when: One shape animates into another to suggest they are the same object.
A scene shows a knot, band or surface being deformed.
The narration uses words such as equivalent, the same, or can be turned into.
intent_signals: morph the mug into the doughnut
show these knots are the same
example_prompts: Animate a deformation that never tears or passes through itself.
Show two knots and whether this animation proves anything.
negative_signals: Artistic morphs with no mathematical claim.
Deformations of physical materials, which are governed by mechanics rather than topology.
not_for: Artistic morphs with no mathematical claim.
Deformations of physical materials, which are governed by mechanics rather than topology.

principles: A morph implemented by interpolating vertices can tear, pinch or self-intersect on the way, and each of those events breaks the property the animation appears to demonstrate. It need not: interpolating between a mesh and its translate stays embedded throughout. What follows is that the intermediate states must be verified for the deformation class you claim, not that vertex interpolation is always wrong.

The strength of the claim depends on what is forbidden during the motion: forbidding tearing and self-intersection makes an animation evidence of an ambient deformation, while allowing them makes it an illustration.

A rendered animation is not by itself a proof: sampled frames show that these configurations were produced, not that no obstruction exists. A mathematically specified family with a justification is different, and can constitute a construction for that particular pair; the honest distinction is between an unverified animation and a specified, checked family.
Stating the claim honestly is cheap and preserves the value of the animation as intuition.
implementation: Decide the class of deformation being demonstrated and enforce it: continuity of the map, embedding without self-intersection, or ambient isotopy.
Prefer a parametrised family of shapes over vertex interpolation, so intermediate states are genuine members of the family.
Detect and report self-intersection during the motion rather than relying on the eye.
Label the animation as illustration when the constraints are not enforced, and say which are violated.
Let the viewer stop anywhere and inspect the intermediate configuration, which is where violations show.
observable_checks: Step through the motion and look for pinches, tears or surfaces passing through each other.
Run a self-intersection test at several intermediate parameter values rather than only at the endpoints.
Confirm intermediate frames are valid shapes of the same kind, not degenerate meshes.
Check that the words on screen match the constraints actually enforced.

creative_affordances: Deliberately impossible morphs are excellent visual devices when labelled as such.
Slow, staged deformations with a hold at the difficult moment often communicate better than a fast morph.
known_limits: Authored claim-scoping guidance; it establishes no topological result and provides no intersection algorithm.
No runtime animation has been inspected for this record.
